# Standard weights and measures (`standard_weights_measures`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by metric_system_units, precision_measurement
- Core idea: One legal set of units for length, volume and weight, defined by master standards kept by the authority, with verified and stamped copies in every market and inspectors who test traders' measures and fine false ones. Where every town has its own bushel and the buyer's measure differs from the seller's, each sale is a dispute and long-distance trade and fair taxation are crippled. Make the standards hard to tamper with (stone, bronze), tie units together (a volume of water defines a weight), use simple ratios, and keep the reference set in a temple or town hall where anyone may check.
- Pitfalls:
  - Decreeing units without distributing copies and inspectors changes nothing; France needed until 1840 to make the metric system stick
  - Old measures encode rents, dues and wages (a heaped or a level bushel): changing them shifts income, so lords and peasants both resist
  - Defining a unit by something not reproducible (the king's foot, a grain of barley) lets it drift; use a made standard or a natural constant that can be re-measured
  - Thinking uniform measures began with the metric system: Indus weights show widespread standardisation, and Qin decrees explicitly required uniform measures
- History: india: c. 2600–1900 BC – Indus cities use cubical chert weights in a fixed series (doubling from about 0.87 g; a common unit near 13.7 g) across the whole civilisation; mesopotamia: c. 2100 BC – Ur-Namma claims to have standardised the mina and the sila measure; inscribed royal stone weights survive from Shulgi's reign; egypt: c. 2700 BC – royal cubit of about 52.4 cm, with master rods and working copies; china: 344 BC – Shang Yang's bronze standard measure; 221 BC Qin Shi Huang imposes uniform weights, measures and axle gauge, with inscribed standards sent to all commanderies; greece: 5th–4th c. BC – Athens keeps official standards and appoints metronomoi to inspect market measures; rome: standard weights and measures kept on the Capitol and in temples, with copies in provincial towns (measuring tables survive at Pompeii); islamic: 8th–9th c. – the muhtasib (market inspector) checks weights, measures and coin; glass weights stamped by the governor in Egypt; americas: 15th c. – Inca officials use standard units of length and volume for state storehouses and labour dues; europe: 1215 – Magna Carta cl. 35 demands one measure of wine, ale and corn; 1795–1799 metric system; 1875 Metre Convention
- Read:
  - Witold Kula, Measures and Men (1986)
  - Ken Alder, The Measure of All Things (2002)
